docs.title: liveplot
docs.text:
Written by Claude

These docs, including the docstrings behind the API reference, were written by Claude (Anthropic's AI model) using Claude Code, from the source. The code is the authority; please open an issue for anything wrong.

Live training curves in Jupyter, Colab and the VS Code / Cursor interactive window, with a tqdm bar underneath, at (almost) no cost to the training loop.

docs.title: Install
docs.text:
pip install "liveplot[notebook] @ git+https://github.com/ARENA-education/liveplot.git"

matplotlib, numpy and pillow are the requirements. The notebook extra adds ipython for the live display and tqdm for the progress bar. A notebook already has both, so plain pip install git+https://github.com/ARENA-education/liveplot.git is enough there.

docs.title: Quickstart
docs.text:
from liveplot import LivePlot

plot = LivePlot(loader, "loss | acc", "lr")   # wrap the loop, like tqdm
plot["acc"].set_ylim(0, 1)                    # configure, like matplotlib
for batch in plot:
    loss, acc = train_step(batch)
    plot.log(loss=loss, acc=acc, lr=lr)       # log, like wandb
  • Wrap the loop. LivePlot(loader) yields the loader's items. Each item moves the x-axis one step and updates the progress bar. plot.log on its own does not move x.
  • Log by name. plot.log(loss=loss) adds a point to the curve loss at the current x. A metric exists from the first time you log it.
  • Lay out with strings. Each string is one panel. Names separated by spaces share a y-axis. Names after | go on a right-hand y-axis. Here loss and acc share a panel with two y-axes, and lr has its own panel. With no strings, every metric shares one panel.
  • Configure with matplotlib's names. plot["acc"] is the y-axis that holds acc.

For nested epoch and batch loops, create the plot once and wrap the inner loop with plot(...). The x-axis continues across epochs:

plot = LivePlot("loss", "acc")
for epoch in range(epochs):
    for batch in plot(loader, desc=f"epoch {epoch}"):
        plot.log(loss=train_step(batch))      # one point per batch
    plot.log(acc=evaluate())                  # one point per epoch
plot.finish()

The plot is drawn by a separate process and shown as a plain image, so it behaves the same in every notebook front end, and interrupting a cell is safe. Everything you log is also kept in plot.data.

docs.title: LivePlot
docs.text:
LivePlot(
    *args,
    total: int | None = None,
    initial: int | float = 0,
    unit: str = "step",
    unit_scale: int | float = 1,
    refresh_seconds: float = 1.0,
    max_cols: int | None = 3,
    rows: int | None = None,
    cols: int | None = None,
    cell_size: tuple = (5, 3.5),
    dpi: int = 100,
    show: bool = True,
    progress: bool = True,
    desc: str | None = None,
    record: bool | str = False,
    smooth: float | None = None,
    fixed_x: bool = False,
    si_xticks: bool = False,
)

A live plot of the metrics you log, with a tqdm progress bar underneath.

Metrics are named when you log them: plot.log(loss=0.3). Each name becomes a curve, and the figure redraws in the notebook's output cell while the loop runs.

The x value of a point is the plot's step counter at the time of the log call. log itself does not advance the counter. Advance it in one of three ways:

  1. Iterate the plot: for batch in LivePlot(loader). Each item advances the counter by one.
  2. Wrap an inner loop with plot(loader), or call plot.update() once per step. Use these for nested epoch and batch loops.
  3. Pass the x value yourself: plot.log(step, loss=0.3).

If you do none of these, every point is logged at the same x (initial, 0 by default) and the curve collapses to a vertical line.

Outside a notebook nothing is drawn, but data still collects everything.

Example 
from liveplot import LivePlot

plot = LivePlot(loader, "loss | acc", "lr")   # two panels; acc on a right-hand axis
plot["acc"].set_ylim(0, 1)
for batch in plot:                            # wrapping the loader advances x
    loss, acc = train_step(batch)
    plot.log(loss=loss, acc=acc, lr=get_lr())

Create a plot: LivePlot([iterable,] *panels, **options).

Parameters:

Name Type Description Default *args Any

An optional iterable, then any number of panel layouts.

The iterable is anything you would loop over: a range, a DataLoader, an existing tqdm bar. If the first argument is not a string or a dict, it is taken as the iterable. Iterating the plot then yields its items, advances x by one per item, shows a progress bar, and calls finish() when the loop ends. An existing tqdm bar is reused, not wrapped in a second one. Leave the iterable out for nested loops and use plot(inner_iterable) or plot.update().

Each layout string is one panel. Names separated by spaces share the left y-axis. Names after a | go on a right-hand y-axis: "loss", "train_loss val_loss", "loss | acc". With no layout, every metric you log shares one panel. With a layout, a metric that no string mentions gets a panel of its own. A dict such as {"metrics": ["acc"], "ylim": (0, 1)} is also accepted in place of a string, but the setters are the intended way to configure a panel.

() total int | None

Number of items in the whole run. Optional. Defaults to len(iterable) when there is an iterable with a length. It does two things. It is the length of the progress bar when the bar cannot get one from the iterable: the bar that update() opens, and the bar for an iterable that has no len(). And with fixed_x=True it fixes the x range. With the default fixed_x=False it does not change the figure. Bars made by plot(iterable) use len(iterable).

None initial int | float

The x value of the first item. Use initial=1 for a 1-based x-axis.

0 unit str

Name of one item. It is the default x label and the unit on the progress bar.

'step' unit_scale int | float

How much x advances per item. x = initial + n * unit_scale. For example unit="examples", unit_scale=batch_size plots against examples seen.

1 refresh_seconds float

Minimum time between redraws. Points that arrive in between are drawn together in the next frame. 0 redraws whenever new data arrives.

1.0 max_cols int | None

Widest grid of panels. None gives a near-square grid.

3 rows int | None

Fix the number of grid rows.

None cols int | None

Fix the number of grid columns.

None cell_size tuple

(width, height) of one panel, in inches.

(5, 3.5) dpi int

Resolution of the rendered image.

100 show bool

False draws nothing. Metrics are still collected in data and shown on the progress bar.

True progress bool

False shows no progress bar.

True desc str | None

Text before the progress bar, for the bar made by iterating the plot or by update(). Bars made by plot(iterable, desc=...) take their own.

None record bool | str

True keeps every rendered frame in frames. A path such as "run.gif" also writes an animated GIF there at finish(). Recording works outside a notebook too.

False smooth float | None

Default smoothing weight for every panel, from 0 up to but not including 1. See set_smooth.

None fixed_x bool

False (the default) lets the x-axis grow with the data. True, with a known total, fixes the x-axis to (initial, initial + total * unit_scale) from the first frame, so the curve grows into an axis that already spans the run. It has no effect without a total.

False si_xticks bool

True labels the x-axis with SI prefixes (100k, 1.5M, 2G, 3T), for long runs whose tick labels would otherwise run into each other, e.g. 300000 examples. Axes below 10,000 are unchanged, and from 1e15 matplotlib's scientific notation is used. False (the default) leaves matplotlib's usual labels.

False

docs.title: panels property
docs.text:
panels: list

The panels of the grid, in order, as a list of Panel.

Example 
plot.panels[0].set_title("training")

docs.title: x_range property
docs.text:
x_range

The fixed x-axis range, or None when the x-axis follows the data.

It is (initial, initial + total * unit_scale) when fixed_x=True and total is known, and None otherwise.

docs.title: step property
docs.text:
step

The x value that a log() call without an explicit step gets right now.

Once a loop is wrapped or update() has been called, this is initial + n * unit_scale. Before that, it is the step of the last log(step, ...) call, or initial if there has been none.

docs.title: subplots classmethod
docs.text:
subplots(
    nrows: int = 1,
    ncols: int = 1,
    *,
    figsize=None,
    squeeze: bool = True,
    width_ratios=None,
    height_ratios=None,
    iterable=None,
    **kwargs,
)

Create a plot with a fixed grid of empty panels, like plt.subplots.

Fill each panel with ax.plot("loss", ...) for curves or ax.imshow(tensor) for an image. The grid never grows: a metric you log without placing it joins the first panel that is still empty, or the first curve panel if none is empty.

Parameters:

Name Type Description Default nrows int

Number of grid rows.

1 ncols int

Number of grid columns.

1 figsize tuple[float, float] | None

(width, height) of the whole figure in inches. Without it, each panel is cell_size inches.

None squeeze bool

True returns one Panel for a 1x1 grid, a flat list for a single row or column, and a 2-d grid otherwise. False always returns the 2-d grid.

True width_ratios Sequence[float] | None

Relative column widths, one per column, e.g. (1, 1.3).

None height_ratios Sequence[float] | None

Relative row heights, one per row.

None iterable Iterable | None

An iterable to wrap, as in LivePlot(iterable).

None **kwargs Any

Any other LivePlot option, such as total or smooth.

{}

Returns:

Type Description tuple[LivePlot, Panel | list[Panel] | _PanelGrid]

(plot, axes), the plot and its panels.

Example 
plot, (ax_loss, ax_samples) = LivePlot.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(11, 4))
ax_loss.plot("lossD", "lossG")           # two metrics on the left axis
ax_loss.twinx().plot("D_real")           # one on the right-hand axis
for batch in plot(loader):
    plot.log(lossD=..., lossG=..., D_real=...)
    if plot.n % 250 == 0:
        ax_samples.imshow(netG(fixed_noise), rows=2, vmin=-1, vmax=1)
plot.finish()

docs.title: __call__
docs.text:
__call__(iterable, **tqdm_kwargs)

Wrap a loop so that each item advances the x-axis by one step: plot(loader).

Use this for nested loops. Create the plot once, then wrap the inner loop on every epoch. The step count continues from one wrapped loop to the next, and each gets its own progress bar of length len(iterable). The count is 0 inside the body for the first item, like for step in range(n). The plot is not finished when the loop ends, so call finish() yourself or use with.

Parameters:

Name Type Description Default iterable Iterable

What to loop over. An existing tqdm bar is reused.

required **tqdm_kwargs Any

Passed to tqdm, e.g. desc="epoch 3".

{}

Yields:

Type Description Any

The items of iterable.

Example 
plot = LivePlot("loss", "acc")
for epoch in range(epochs):
    for batch in plot(loader, desc=f"epoch {epoch}"):
        plot.log(loss=train_step(batch))     # one point per batch
    plot.log(acc=evaluate())                 # one point per epoch
plot.finish()

docs.title: update
docs.text:
update(n=1)

Advance the x-axis by hand, like tqdm's update.

Use this when you do not want to wrap the loop. Call it once per step, after logging that step's metrics. The first call opens one progress bar for the whole run, of length total if you gave one, and finish() closes it.

Parameters:

Name Type Description Default n int

How many items to advance by.

1 Example 
plot = LivePlot(total=epochs * len(loader))   # total only sets the bar's length
for epoch in range(epochs):
    plot.set_description(f"epoch {epoch}")
    for batch in loader:
        plot.log(loss=train_step(batch))
        plot.update()
plot.finish()

docs.title: __iter__
docs.text:
__iter__()

Iterate over the iterable given to the constructor: for batch in plot.

Each item advances the x-axis by one step, a progress bar is shown, and finish() is called when the loop ends, including when it ends with break or an exception. Raises TypeError if the plot was created without an iterable.

docs.title: log
docs.text:
log(*args, **metrics)

Record one value for each of one or more metrics.

A metric is created the first time you log it. Each call adds one point per metric, at the plot's current x (plot.step). Metrics can be logged at different rates: each keeps its own list of points.

log does not advance x. Wrap the loop (for batch in plot or plot(loader)), call plot.update(), or pass the step as the first argument. Otherwise every point has the same x.

Parameters:

Name Type Description Default *args Any

Optionally the x value for this call, then optionally a dict of metrics: log(step, loss=0.3), log(step, {"loss": 0.3}) or log({"loss": 0.3}). In a wrapped loop an explicit step applies to this call only. With no wrapped loop it also becomes the x of later calls that give no step.

() **metrics float

Metric values by name: log(loss=0.3, acc=0.9). A value is anything float() accepts, including a one-element tensor.

{} Example 
plot = LivePlot(range(1000), "loss | acc")
for step in plot:
    plot.log(loss=train_step())      # every step
    if step % 50 == 0:
        plot.log(acc=evaluate())     # every 50 steps, same x-axis

docs.title: axhline
docs.text:
axhline(y, label=None, *, metric=None, **kwargs)

Draw a horizontal reference line.

With metric, the line goes on the axis that holds that metric, the same as plot[metric].axhline(y, label). Without it, the line goes on the left axis of every panel that exists now. Panels created later do not get it. The line is dashed grey by default and has a legend entry.

Parameters:

Name Type Description Default y float

Where to draw the line.

required label str | None

The legend text. Defaults to the value of y.

None metric str | None

Draw the line only on the axis holding this metric.

None **kwargs Any

Passed to matplotlib's Axes.axhline (color, linestyle, linewidth, alpha, ...).

{} Example 
plot.axhline(math.log(d_vocab), "uniform", metric="loss")

docs.text:
axvline(x=None, label=None, **kwargs)

Draw a vertical line on every curve panel, including panels created later.

The line is dotted grey by default. For one panel only, use Panel.axvline.

Parameters:

Name Type Description Default x float | None

Where to draw the line. Defaults to the current step (plot.step) at the time of the call.

None label str | None

Text written along the line. It does not go in the legend.

None **kwargs Any

Passed to matplotlib's Axes.axvline (color, linestyle, ...).

{} Example 
if step == warmup_steps:
    plot.axvline(label="warmup ends")

docs.title: imshow
docs.text:
imshow(x, **kwargs)

Show an image, or a batch of images as a grid, replacing the previous one.

The picture goes on the plot's first image panel. If the plot has none, one is added. On a plot made by subplots, an image panel must already exist, so call imshow on a panel there first.

Parameters:

Name Type Description Default x ArrayLike

A torch tensor, numpy array or other array-like. See Panel.imshow for the accepted shapes.

required **kwargs Any

Passed to Panel.imshow (rows, cols, vmin, vmax, ...).

{}

Returns:

Type Description Panel

The panel that holds the image.

Example 
plot = LivePlot(range(steps))
for step in plot:
    plot.log(loss=train_step())
    if step % 100 == 0:
        plot.imshow(model(holdout), vmin=0, vmax=1)

docs.title: figure
docs.text:
figure()

Build a matplotlib Figure of the plot as it stands.

The figure has the same panels, data, reference lines and images as the live plot. It is built from data on the calling thread and is separate from the live display, so changing it does not change the live plot. It works during or after the run, and also with show=False or outside a notebook.

Returns:

Type Description Figure

A new figure.

Example 
fig = plot.figure()
fig.suptitle("run 12")
fig.savefig("run12.png", dpi=150)

docs.title: refresh
docs.text:
refresh()

Redraw now, if drawing happens on the calling thread (mode == "thread").

In the usual mode a separate process draws on its own schedule and this does nothing.

docs.title: finish
docs.text:
finish()

Draw the final frame, close the progress bar and stop the render process.

Iterating the plot (for batch in plot) and the with block call this for you. Call it yourself after nested loops that use plot(loader) or plot.update(). Calling it twice is safe. data stays available afterwards. If record was a path, the GIF is written here.

docs.title: __enter__
docs.text:
__enter__()

Use the plot as a context manager: finish() is called when the block exits.

Example 
with LivePlot("loss") as plot:
    for step in range(num_steps):
        plot.log(step, loss=train_step())

docs.title: Panel
docs.text:
Panel(plot, index: int)

One panel of the grid: a set of curves with one or two y-axes, or one image.

You do not create these. Get one from plot.panels[i], from plot[metric].panel, or from LivePlot.subplots, which returns the panels of a fixed grid.

A panel has a title, an x-axis, a legend and a smoothing weight, and up to two y-axes: panel.left and panel.right. The y setters on the panel itself (set_ylabel, set_ylim, set_yscale, axhline) act on the left axis.

Setters can be called before the loop or during it. The figure is laid out again on the next frame.

Example 
plot = LivePlot(loader, "loss | acc", "lr")
plot.panels[0].set_title("training")
plot.panels[0].right.set_ylim(0, 1)   # the axis holding acc
plot.panels[1].set_yscale("log")      # the lr panel

twinx() -> _Axis

Return this panel's right-hand y-axis, like matplotlib's Axes.twinx.

docs.title: imshow
docs.text:
imshow(
    x,
    *,
    rows=None,
    cols=None,
    griddim=None,
    vmin=None,
    vmax=None,
    scale_each=False,
    channels=None,
    cmap="gray",
    padding=0,
    pad_value=0,
    max_images=64,
    max_cols=8,
)

Show an image, or a batch of images as a grid, on this panel.

Each call replaces the previous picture. Once the plot has a step (a loop is wrapped or something has been logged), the panel's title shows the step the picture was drawn at.

Accepted shapes: (H, W), (1, H, W), (H, W, 3|4), (B, H, W), (B, 1|3|4, H, W) and (B, H, W, 1|3|4). (3, H, W) and (4, H, W) are ambiguous and raise ValueError; pass channels. A 3-d array whose last dimension is 3 or 4 is read as one colour image.

Parameters:

Name Type Description Default x ArrayLike

A torch tensor, numpy array, or anything numpy.asarray accepts. Tensors are detached and moved to the CPU for you.

required rows int | None

Number of grid rows. The number of columns is inferred.

None cols int | None

Number of grid columns. The number of rows is inferred.

None griddim tuple[int, int] | None

(rows, cols), fixing both. Missing cells are left blank and extra images are dropped. Do not combine with rows or cols.

None vmin float | None

Value at the dark end of the range. Defaults to the minimum of the batch.

None vmax float | None

Value at the bright end of the range. Defaults to the maximum of the batch. Fixing vmin and vmax stops the brightness changing from frame to frame. They apply to colour images too. uint8 input is shown as it is unless one of them is given.

None scale_each bool

Scale each image to its own range instead of the batch's.

False channels str | None

How to read a 3-d input: "first" for (C, H, W), "last" for (H, W, C), "none" for a batch of grayscale (B, H, W).

None cmap str

Matplotlib colormap for grayscale images.

'gray' padding int

Pixels of pad_value around every image in a grid. 0 puts them edge to edge.

0 pad_value int

The value (0 to 255) of padding pixels and blank cells.

0 max_images int | None

Show only this many images from the batch, with a warning. None shows all of them.

64 max_cols int | None

Widest grid to choose when neither rows, cols nor griddim is given. The default grid is near-square: 3 images give 2x2, 8 give 3x3, 64 give 8x8.

8

docs.title: _Axis
docs.text:
_Axis(plot, index: int, right: bool)

One y-axis of a panel: the left one, or the right-hand one.

You do not create these. plot["acc"] returns the axis that holds the metric acc, whichever side it is on. panel.left, panel.right and panel.twinx() return a panel's axes directly.

The y setters (set_ylabel, set_ylim, set_yscale, axhline) act on this axis only. The other setters (set_title, set_xlabel, set_xlim, set_smooth, axvline, legend) act on the panel the axis belongs to, because a panel's two y-axes share one title, x-axis and legend.

Setters can be called before the loop or during it. The figure is laid out again on the next frame.

Example 
plot = LivePlot(loader, "loss | acc")
plot["acc"].set_ylim(0, 1)            # the right-hand axis
plot["loss"].set_yscale("log")        # the left-hand axis

docs.text: _PanelGrid in the source; what LivePlot.subplots returns for grids of at least 2 x 2.

docs.title: _PanelGrid
docs.text:
_PanelGrid(rows: list)

The 2-d grid of panels that LivePlot.subplots returns for two or more rows and columns.

It is indexed like matplotlib's array of axes: axes[0][1] and axes[0, 1] are the same panel. Iterating it yields rows, each a list of panels, so it unpacks like a nested list.

Example 
plot, axes = LivePlot.subplots(2, 2)
axes[0, 0].plot("loss")
(ax_a, ax_b), (ax_c, ax_d) = axes

(rows, columns).

docs.title: Is total needed?
docs.text:
No. total is tqdm's: the length of the run. It sets the progress bar's length when the bar can't get one from len(), and, with fixed_x=True, fixes the x-axis to the whole run. fixed_x is off by default, so the figure is the same with or without total.

LivePlot(loader) takes total from len(loader). Bars made by plot(loader) always use len(loader). See The x-axis and total.

docs.title: Why wrap the dataloader?
docs.text:
Wrapping moves x. plot.log records values but doesn't advance x, so with nothing advancing it every point lands at x = 0: a vertical line, not a curve.

Three ways to advance x:

# 1. Wrap the loop (also gives a progress bar)
for batch in plot(loader):
    plot.log(loss=train_step(batch))

# 2. Call update() once per step
for batch in loader:
    plot.log(loss=train_step(batch))
    plot.update()

# 3. Pass the step yourself
for step, batch in enumerate(loader):
    plot.log(step, loss=train_step(batch))

Call plot.finish() after each. See The x-axis and total.

docs.title: Two metrics on one axis?
docs.text: One string, names separated by a space: LivePlot(loader, "train_loss val_loss"). With no strings at all, every metric shares one panel.

docs.title: A metric on the right-hand axis?
docs.text: Put it after |: LivePlot(loader, "loss | acc"). Then plot["acc"] is the right-hand axis. Each side can hold several names: "lossD lossG | acc".

docs.title: Several panels?
docs.text:
One string per panel:

LivePlot(loader, "loss", "acc", "lr")                  # three panels
LivePlot(loader, "train_loss val_loss | acc", "lr")    # two, the first with two y-axes

A metric no string mentions gets its own panel. See Panels and layout strings.

docs.title: Why is nothing drawn?
docs.text: The plot only shows in a notebook (Jupyter, Colab, VS Code / Cursor interactive window). In a script nothing is drawn, silently. plot.data and plot.figure() still work.

docs.title: Do I need finish()?
docs.text: Not for for batch in plot or with LivePlot(...) as plot:; both finish for you. After plot(loader) or plot.update() loops, call plot.finish(): it draws the last frame, closes the bar and stops the render process.

docs.title: Guide
docs.text:
One feature per page. Start with the x-axis.

  • The x-axis and total: what advances x; total, fixed_x, initial, unit, unit_scale, si_xticks.
  • Panels and layout strings: one string per panel, | for a right-hand axis, the grid.
  • Logging at different rates: per-step beside per-epoch metrics; reading values back; show=False.
  • Customising axes: titles, labels, limits, scales, markers, with matplotlib's names.
  • Reference lines: axhline and axvline.
  • Images with subplots and imshow: samples beside the loss curves.
  • Smoothing and log axes: wandb's EMA, log y-axes.
  • Saving and recording: a matplotlib figure, a GIF of the run.
  • How it works: the render process, the bar, interrupts, scripts.

Every class and method: API reference.

docs.title: Customising axes
docs.text: Setters use matplotlib's names. Call them before or during the loop; the next frame picks them up.

docs.title: Which object to call
docs.text:
Object Get it with Changes Axis plot["acc"] The y-axis holding that metric, left or right Panel plot.panels[0], plot["acc"].panel One panel, and its left axis Plot plot Every panel, including later ones 
plot = LivePlot(loader, "loss | acc", "lr")

plot["acc"].set_ylim(0, 1)                   # right-hand axis of panel 0
plot["acc"].set_ylabel("test accuracy")
plot["lr"].set_yscale("log")

plot.panels[0].set_title("training")         # one panel
plot.panels[0].set_xlim(0, 10_000)

plot.set_xlabel("batches")                   # every panel

plot[metric] finds the axis on either side. panel.left / panel.right name the two axes directly.

docs.title: The setters
docs.text:
Axis (reference):

Setter Effect set_ylabel(text) y label set_ylim(low, high) Fix the y range; also takes one (low, high). Both required. set_yscale("log") "linear" or "log" set_marker("o") A dot on every point, e.g. a once-per-epoch eval. None turns it off. axhline(y, label) Horizontal reference line

Panel (reference):

Setter Effect set_title(text) Title set_xlabel(text) x label set_xlim(low, high) Fix the x range set_smooth(weight) Smoothing legend(**kwargs) Move/restyle the legend; kwargs go to Axes.legend axvline(x, label) Vertical reference line

Panel setters also work on an axis (acting on its panel): plot["acc"].set_title("evaluation"). Axis y setters also work on a panel (acting on its left axis).

On the plot, set_title, set_xlabel, set_xlim, set_ylabel, set_ylim, set_yscale and set_smooth apply to every panel; the y setters reach left axes only.

docs.title: Several at once
docs.text:
set(**kwargs), like Axes.set: name=value calls set_name(value).

plot["acc"].set(ylabel="test accuracy", ylim=(0, 1))
plot.panels[0].set(title="training", xlabel="examples")
plot.set(xlabel="examples", smooth=0.9)       # every panel

docs.title: Moving the legend
docs.text:
plot.panels[0].legend(loc="upper left")
plot.panels[0].legend(loc="upper center", bbox_to_anchor=(0.5, -0.15), ncols=3)   # below the panel

docs.title: Not supported
docs.text: One-sided limits, and scales other than "linear" / "log". For those, take plot.figure() and change it in matplotlib.

docs.title: A separate render process
docs.text:
plot.log appends numbers and queues them; it never draws.

A separate process owns the matplotlib figure. It redraws at most every refresh_seconds (default 1.0), only when there's new data; points in between share a frame. refresh_seconds=0 redraws on every arrival.

Each frame comes back as a PNG and replaces the image in the output cell. No widgets, no JavaScript, so Jupyter, Colab, VS Code and Cursor all behave the same. A background thread shows each frame as soon as it's ready, so rarely-logging loops still update on time.

If the render process can't start, liveplot warns and draws inside log instead. plot.mode is "process", "thread", or "off" (nothing drawn).

docs.title: Progress bar
docs.text: tqdm's (tqdm.auto), under the plot, with the latest metrics as its postfix. Pass your own tqdm bar as the iterable to reuse it. progress=False turns it off.

docs.title: Interrupting
docs.text:
Safe. Jupyter interrupts every process the kernel started; the render process ignores it. You keep the last frame and plot.data. Rerunning the cell starts a new plot.

A plot dropped without finish() stops its render process when garbage-collected. The render process also exits if the kernel dies.

docs.title: Outside a notebook
docs.text: Nothing is drawn, silently. plot.data, plot.latest, the bar, plot.figure() and recording still work.

docs.title: Dependencies
docs.text: import liveplot imports nothing heavy; matplotlib, numpy and pillow load on first use. IPython and tqdm are optional: without IPython nothing is shown, without tqdm there's no bar.

docs.title: Images with subplots and imshow
docs.text: A panel can hold a picture instead of curves: loss curves every step beside generated samples now and then.

docs.title: LivePlot.subplots
docs.text:
LivePlot.subplots follows plt.subplots: it returns the plot and a fixed grid of empty panels, which you then fill.

plot, (ax_loss, ax_samples) = LivePlot.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(11, 4))
ax_loss.plot("lossD", "lossG")            # these metrics on the left axis
ax_loss.twinx().plot("D_real")            # this one on the right
ax_samples.set_title("generator samples")

for epoch in range(epochs):
    for imgs, _ in plot(loader, desc=f"epoch {epoch}"):
        lossD, lossG, d_real = train_step(imgs)
        plot.log(lossD=lossD, lossG=lossG, D_real=d_real)                     # every step
        if plot.n % 250 == 0:
            ax_samples.imshow(netG(fixed_noise), rows=2, vmin=-1, vmax=1)     # replaces the last picture
plot.finish()
  • ax.plot(...) takes metric names, not data; values come from plot.log.
  • ax.twinx() is the right-hand axis.
  • figsize is the whole figure, in inches. width_ratios / height_ratios as in matplotlib.
  • Other kwargs go to LivePlot (total, smooth, …). For a single loop, pass iterable=loader.

The grid never grows. An unplaced metric joins the first empty panel, else the first curve panel.

docs.title: What subplots returns
docs.text:
matplotlib's squeeze rules:

Grid axes is 1 x 1 one panel one row or column a flat list larger a 2-d grid: axes[0][1], axes[0, 1], axes.flat

squeeze=False always gives the 2-d grid.

docs.title: plot.imshow
docs.text:
For one picture, plot.imshow adds an image panel on first call; later calls replace the picture.

plot = LivePlot(range(steps))
for step in plot:
    plot.log(loss=train_step())
    if step % 100 == 0:
        plot.imshow(model(holdout))

On a subplots plot, call imshow on a panel instead.

docs.title: Accepted input
docs.text:
Torch tensors (detached and moved to CPU for you; torch is never imported), numpy arrays, array-likes.

Shape Read as (H, W), (1, H, W) one grayscale image (H, W, 3), (H, W, 4) one colour image, channels last (B, H, W) B grayscale images (B, 1|3|4, H, W) B images, channels first (torch) (B, H, W, 1|3|4) B images, channels last

(3, H, W) and (4, H, W) are ambiguous and raise: pass channels="first" (one colour image) or channels="none" (grayscale batch). A grayscale batch of images 3 or 4 pixels wide also needs channels="none".

docs.title: Grids
docs.text:
• rows=2 or cols=5 fixes one side; the other is inferred.
  • griddim=(rows, cols) fixes both; blanks fill, extras are dropped.
  • Default: near-square, at most max_cols (8) wide.
  • At most max_images (64) shown, with a warning; max_images=None for all.
  • Edge to edge by default; padding=2 adds 2 px of pad_value around each.

docs.title: Scaling
docs.text:
Default: batch min is black, batch max white.

  • vmin / vmax fix the range. Do this for live views, or brightness jumps between frames.
  • scale_each=True scales each image alone.
  • uint8 is shown as is, unless vmin / vmax is given.

Unlike matplotlib's imshow, vmin / vmax apply to colour images too. For a tanh generator use vmin=-1, vmax=1.

docs.title: Step in the title
docs.text:
Image panel titles show the step the picture was drawn at, e.g. "generator samples (step 250)", so you can tell how old it is.

Full example: examples/dcgan_synthetic.py, a fake DCGAN run.

docs.title: What log accepts
docs.text:
plot.log(loss=0.3, acc=0.9)          # at the current x
plot.log(step, loss=0.3)             # at an explicit x
plot.log(step, {"loss": 0.3})        # a dict, for names that aren't identifiers
plot.log({"loss": 0.3})              # a dict at the current x

Values are anything float() accepts, including one-element tensors. Pass loss.item() or loss.detach(): PyTorch warns when converting a tensor that requires grad. See plot.log.

docs.title: Different rates
docs.text:
Each metric keeps its own (x, value) points, and log adds one to each metric it names. A metric logged every 50 steps simply has fewer points, on the same x-axis:

plot = LivePlot(range(num_steps), "loss | eval_loss eval_acc")
for step in plot:
    plot.log(loss=train_step())                              # every step
    if step % 50 == 0:
        eval_loss, eval_acc = evaluate()
        plot.log(eval_loss=eval_loss, eval_acc=eval_acc)     # every 50 steps

Sparse curves read better with a dot on each point: plot["eval_acc"].set_marker("o").

docs.title: Once per epoch
docs.text:
Log after the inner loop. x is the count reached, i.e. batches so far:

plot = LivePlot("loss", "acc")
for epoch in range(epochs):
    for batch in plot(loader, desc=f"epoch {epoch}"):
        plot.log(loss=train_step(batch))
    plot.log(acc=evaluate())      # at x = (epoch + 1) * len(loader)
plot.finish()

docs.title: Reading values back
docs.text:
• plot.data: full history, {metric: (xs, values)}.
  • plot.latest: the last value of each metric.

Both fill whether or not anything is drawn.

xs, losses = plot.data["loss"]
best = min(losses)

docs.title: Collecting without drawing
docs.text: show=False draws nothing; metrics are still collected and the bar still runs. progress=False turns the bar off. The two are independent.

docs.title: Panels and layout strings
docs.text: The figure is a grid of panels. A panel holds curves on one or two y-axes.

docs.title: No layout
docs.text:
Metrics exist once logged. With no layout, all share one panel with a legend:

plot = LivePlot(range(300))
for step in plot:
    plot.log(loss=..., val_loss=...)    # one panel, two curves

docs.title: Layout strings
docs.text:
One string per panel, after the iterable if any:

plot = LivePlot(loader, "loss", "return | entropy", "lossD lossG | acc")
  • Space-separated names share the left y-axis.
  • Names after | go on a right-hand y-axis. At most one |.
String Left Right "loss" loss — "return | entropy" return entropy "lossD lossG | acc" lossD, lossG acc

Names in a string can't contain spaces or |.

A logged metric that no string mentions gets a new panel at the end:

plot = LivePlot(loader, "loss")
plot.log(loss=0.3, lr=1e-3)     # lr gets its own panel

docs.title: Defaults
docs.text:
• Title: the metric names joined by " / ".
  • x label: the plot's unit ("step").
  • y labels: only on two-axis panels, the metric names of each side.
  • A legend on every panel, covering both axes.

Change any of them with the setters in Customising axes.

docs.title: The grid
docs.text:
Panels fill row by row, at most 3 columns by default.

Option Effect max_cols Widest grid. Default 3; None for near-square. rows Fix the number of rows. cols Fix the number of columns. cell_size (width, height) of one panel, inches. Default (5, 3.5). dpi Image resolution. Default 100. 
plot = LivePlot(loader, "loss", "acc", "lr", "grad_norm", cols=2, cell_size=(4, 3))

For a fixed grid you fill panel by panel, like plt.subplots, use LivePlot.subplots; see Images.

docs.title: The dict form
docs.text: A dict also works in place of a string: {"metrics": ["acc"], "ylim": (0, 1), "ylabel": "test accuracy"}. It's the older form; prefer the setters.

docs.title: Reference lines
docs.text: matplotlib's names: axhline for a level to reach, axvline for a moment in the run.

docs.title: Horizontal
docs.text:
Call axhline on the metric's axis:

plot["loss"].axhline(math.log(d_vocab), "uniform")       # loss of a uniform guess
plot["return"].axhline(500, "solved", color="green")
  • Dashed grey by default; extra kwargs (color, linestyle, linewidth, alpha) go to matplotlib.
  • The label goes in the legend. Without one, the legend shows the number.
  • Drawn on the scale of the axis you called it on, so plot["acc"].axhline(0.9) uses the right axis if acc is there.

plot.axhline(y, label) draws on the left axis of every panel that exists now (not later ones). plot.axhline(y, label, metric="loss") equals plot["loss"].axhline(y, label).

docs.title: Vertical
docs.text:
plot.axvline(label="lr drop")                   # every panel, at the current step
plot.panels[1].axvline(2000, "checkpoint")      # one panel, at x = 2000
  • No x: drawn at plot.step at call time, so you can mark an event where it happens.
  • Dotted grey by default; extra kwargs go to matplotlib.
  • The label is written along the line, not in the legend.
  • plot.axvline covers every curve panel, including later ones. Image panels are skipped.
for step in plot:
    if step == warmup_steps:
        plot.axvline(label="warmup ends")
    plot.log(loss=train_step())

docs.title: A matplotlib figure
docs.text:
plot.figure() returns a matplotlib Figure of the current state: panels, curves, reference lines, images.

fig = plot.figure()
fig.suptitle("run 12")
fig.savefig("run12.png", dpi=150)

Built from plot.data on each call and separate from the live display. Works during or after the run, in a script, and with show=False.

docs.title: Recording a GIF
docs.text:
record="run.gif" keeps every drawn frame and writes a GIF at finish(), replaying at the run's pace. Works in scripts too.

plot = LivePlot(range(steps), "loss | acc", record="run.gif")
for step in plot:
    plot.log(loss=train_step())

record=True keeps frames without writing; write later with plot.save_gif:

plot = LivePlot(range(steps), record=True)
...
plot.save_gif("run.gif", speedup=2.0)     # twice as fast as the run
  • plot.frames: (seconds since creation, PNG bytes) pairs.
  • plot.last_png: the latest frame.
  • One frame per redraw, so refresh_seconds sets the frame count.

docs.title: Smoothing
docs.text:
set_smooth draws a smoothed curve over the faded raw values.

plot.set_smooth(0.9)                  # every panel
plot.panels[0].set_smooth(0.9)        # one panel
plot["loss"].set_smooth(0.9)          # loss's panel
plot = LivePlot(loader, smooth=0.9)   # default for every panel
  • Weight in [0, 1); larger is smoother, 0 is off.
  • Per panel: every curve on it, both axes.
  • Drawing only: plot.data stays raw.

It's wandb's default, the time-weighted EMA, with the same weight as wandb's slider. As in wandb, smoothing depends on how points spread over the x range, not their count. The x range is the data so far, so short runs are barely smoothed and the curve can shift as the run grows. With fixed_x=True and a total, the range is the whole run from the start.

docs.title: Log axes
docs.text:
plot["loss"].set_yscale("log")        # loss's axis
plot.set_yscale("log")                # left axis of every panel

"linear" or "log"; y only.

docs.title: x is a step counter
docs.text:
plot.n counts items consumed, like tqdm's n. A point's x is

x = initial + n * unit_scale

when log is called. n is 0 for the first item and goes up by one after each. The items themselves are never looked at. log doesn't change n.

docs.title: Wrap the loop
docs.text:
Single loop: pass the iterable and iterate the plot. One progress bar; the plot finishes when the loop ends.

plot = LivePlot(loader, "loss")
for batch in plot:
    plot.log(loss=train_step(batch))

Nested loops: create the plot once, wrap the inner loop with plot(...). The count carries across epochs. Each wrapped loop gets its own bar; keyword arguments such as desc go to tqdm.

plot = LivePlot("loss", "acc")
for epoch in range(epochs):
    for batch in plot(loader, desc=f"epoch {epoch}"):
        plot.log(loss=train_step(batch))
    plot.log(acc=evaluate())
plot.finish()

An existing tqdm bar passed as the iterable is reused, not wrapped: LivePlot(tqdm(loader), "loss").

docs.title: Call update()
docs.text:
plot.update() adds one to the count, like tqdm's. Call it after logging the step. The first call opens one bar for the whole run.

plot = LivePlot("loss", total=epochs * len(loader))
for epoch in range(epochs):
    plot.set_description(f"epoch {epoch}")
    for batch in loader:
        plot.log(loss=train_step(batch))
        plot.update()
plot.finish()

docs.title: Pass the step yourself
docs.text:
with LivePlot("loss") as plot:
    for step in range(num_steps):
        plot.log(step, loss=train_step())

No counting, no bar. The step can be any number (examples seen, seconds). Inside a wrapped loop it applies to that call only; otherwise later calls without a step reuse it.

docs.title: None of these
docs.text: Every point lands at x = initial (0), and the figure is a vertical line: plot.data["loss"][0] == [0, 0, 0, ...].

docs.title: total and fixed_x
docs.text:
total is the number of items in the run. Optional.

You write total is LivePlot(range(1000)), LivePlot(loader) len() LivePlot("loss", total=epochs * len(loader)) what you gave LivePlot("loss") None

It sets:

  • The bar's length, when the bar can't get one from len(): the bar from plot.update(), or a generator. Then the bar shows a percentage and ETA. Bars from plot(loader) use len(loader), not total.
  • The x range, only with fixed_x=True: (initial, initial + total * unit_scale) from the first frame, filled from the left.

fixed_x is off by default: the x-axis grows with the data. Without a total it does nothing. For one panel, use set_xlim.

plot = LivePlot(range(1000), "loss", fixed_x=True)                  # x is 0 to 1000 throughout
plot = LivePlot("loss", total=epochs * len(loader), fixed_x=True)   # same, nested loops

docs.title: initial, unit, unit_scale
docs.text:
tqdm's arguments, tqdm's meaning:

  • initial: x of the first item. initial=1 for 1-based; initial=10 plots range(10, 20) at its values.
  • unit: the name of one item. Default x label and bar unit. Default "step".
  • unit_scale: x per item.

Plot against examples seen:

plot = LivePlot(loader, "loss", unit="examples", unit_scale=batch_size)

x is then 0, batch_size, 2 * batch_size, …; the bar shows the same numbers.

docs.title: Reading the current x
docs.text: plot.step: the x a log call would get now. plot.n: the raw count.

docs.title: si_xticks
docs.text:
Default tick labels are matplotlib's, written in full up to a million, so long runs get crowded labels. si_xticks=True uses SI prefixes:

plot = LivePlot("loss", total=epochs * len(loader), unit="examples", unit_scale=batch_size, si_xticks=True)
# x ticks: 0, 50k, 100k, ... 300k

One prefix per axis, from its largest tick: k, M, G, T. Axes below 10,000 are unchanged. From 10¹⁵, matplotlib's scientific notation. LivePlot.subplots takes it too.
